name: Custom chin implant (silicone/Medpor)

lead: A chin implant is a shaped piece of silicone or porous polyethylene (Medpor) placed over the chin bone to push a recessed chin forward. It gives a stronger, more balanced side profile, and can also add height or width.

The implant sits on the front of the jawbone and adds bulk through a cut under the chin or inside the lower lip. Silicone is smooth and removable; porous polyethylene allows tissue ingrowth. Custom implants are designed from a CT scan of the individual's jaw. It is a long-established cosmetic operation, often done alongside nose surgery, and outcomes are documented mainly in surgical case series.

paras: People usually see a surgeon for a consultation and imaging, then have a short operation under anaesthetic. It is often chosen as a less invasive alternative to a sliding genioplasty, and is frequently combined with rhinoplasty. Swelling settles over weeks and the final profile is visible once healed. Forum users compare stock implants with custom designs and discuss whether an implant is enough for a very recessed chin.

Reported risks include swelling, hematoma, infection, implant displacement, bone changes under the implant and nerve numbness. Complication rates depend on technique and surgeon experience. Implants can shift or be removed later, and porous polyethylene is harder to remove than silicone. It is an Rx surgical procedure performed by licensed surgeons.

angle.text: A chin implant adds projection, and sometimes height or width, to a recessed chin by placing material over the chin bone. The stronger, more balanced profile is visible once healed. Silicone, porous polyethylene and patient-specific designs are used, with outcomes documented in surgical case series.

lead: A chin implant is an alloplastic (synthetic) device placed over the lower border of the mandible to increase the projection, and sometimes the height or width, of the chin. Common materials are silicone, porous high-density polyethylene (often sold as Medpor), expanded polytetrafluoroethylene and, more recently, patient-specific implants made from materials such as PEEK. [1][2]

The operation is commonly performed together with rhinoplasty or a facelift. Surgical reviews describe a continuing debate over whether an implant or an osseous (bone-cutting) genioplasty is the better operation for a given patient, and state that complication avoidance depends on technique and surgeon experience. [3][1]

In looksmaxxing communities, chin implants are discussed as a lower-cost, less invasive option than sliding genioplasty, and the term 'custom implant' refers to a design made from the person's own CT scan. A small number of registered trials have compared patient-specific implants with computer-guided genioplasty. [4][2][5]
infobox: Under the chin or inside the lower lip
Removable, more difficult with porous materials

paras: Encyclopedic summaries list silicone as the most common material, noting it can be removed and can shift or be associated with bone resorption; porous polyethylene (Medpor), into which tissue grows and which is harder to remove; ePTFE, fixed with titanium screws; and donor-derived dermal grafts. [1]

Custom or patient-specific implants are designed from a CT scan and fabricated to the individual's anatomy. Registered trials have examined PEEK patient-specific implants for chin deficiency (microgenia). [2]

A review of complications in chin augmentation states that there has been much debate about whether implant placement or osseous genioplasty is superior. [3] An encyclopedia summary states that bone-based osteotomy usually gives a more dramatic correction than a prosthetic implant. [1]
On looksmax.org, users discuss the choice between implant and genioplasty, including cost, reversibility, and whether an implant can substitute for waiting for a bone-moving operation.
Common effects are swelling, bruising and temporary numbness or lip weakness; less common risks include infection, implant displacement, bone changes, and nerve injury. [3][1]
A 1981 clinical analysis of alloplastic chin implants in the otolaryngology literature is one of the early published series examining the outcomes of implant mentoplasty. [6]

Forum threads include questions about whether a chin implant is 'enough' on its own, whether implants suit people with a recessed chin and short face, and requests for ratings of before-and-after photographs. [7]

Some users ask about vertical lengthening via an implant versus a genioplasty.  Others discuss fat grafting as an alternative to either option; the surgical literature describes autologous fat grafting to the chin as an adjunct in facial rejuvenation. [8]

Published surgical literature on chin augmentation is mainly narrative reviews and case series. [3][6] A registered trial (NCT04817930, completed, 20 participants) compared a patient-specific alloplastic chin implant with computer-guided genioplasty, assessing soft-tissue results after one year. [4] Other registered trials have examined the accuracy of patient-specific PEEK implants and of patient-specific implants in genioplasty. [2][5]
